transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?
My sleep has been messed up for a long time now. No matter how I try to change my schedule around, I just can’t seem to get any real rest.
If you are able to sleep on your own preferred schedule (like on weekends or days off), do you sleep well, or do you still struggle to fall or stay asleep?

Even on my days off when I can go to bed on time, I still really struggle to get good sleep. I usually lie awake for an hour or more with my mind racing about my work quotas and homework, and I end up waking up multiple times during the night. Even when I try to sleep in, it never seems to make me feel recharged.
Do you have any physical medical conditions, chronic pain, or breathing issues like loud snoring that might be causing your sleep problems?

No, I don't have any physical medical conditions or chronic pain that I know of. I also don't think I have any breathing issues or loud snoring when I sleep. It really just feels like my mind won't shut off.
Are you currently taking any regular medications, or do you regularly use substances like caffeine, alcohol, or nicotine close to bedtime?
No, I'm not taking any regular medications right now. I also don't use nicotine or alcohol, and I try to avoid caffeine close to bedtime so it doesn't make my sleep any worse.
How many nights a week do you typically experience these sleep difficulties, and how many months or years has this been going on?

With my rotating shifts, my sleep is constantly disrupted pretty much every night of the week. This has been going on steadily for a little over two years now—about two years and four months—starting shortly after I began my QA inspector job.

Do you feel your sleep problems are mainly because your rotating work shifts constantly change your sleep times, or do you think you would still struggle to sleep even if you had a stable, regular daytime schedule every day?

I think I would still struggle even if I had a stable, regular schedule. While the rotating shifts definitely make it harder to set a routine, the real issue is that my mind still races with worries about work quotas and schoolwork even when I'm in bed on time. I would still end up waking up multiple times and feeling completely unrefreshed.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot during the day or as bedtime approaches about whether you'll be able to sleep, and how tired you'll be the next day?
No, I don't really worry about the sleep itself or how tired I'll be the next day. Instead, my mind just races with thoughts about my work quotas and homework whenever I try to lie down and rest.
How does this lack of sleep affect you during the day? For example, does it impact your mood, concentration, or ability to perform at work and school?

Honestly, I feel this constant low, gray heaviness in the background, and I'm so exhausted that even simple things like doing laundry or staying focused in class take way too much effort. It has definitely impacted my performance, as I've started turning in my school assignments late and calling out or swapping my work shifts more often.
You mentioned feeling a constant low, gray heaviness. Have you also lost interest or pleasure in activities you normally enjoy, or felt down and hopeless most of the day?

Yes, I've completely lost interest in the things I used to love. I've stopped going to my basketball league games, dancing nights, and STEM volunteering because I just don't have the energy or excitement for them anymore. Most days, I feel like I'm just going through the motions at work and school without ever really feeling genuinely happy about anything.
Have you felt this low, gray heaviness almost every day for the entire two years, or have there been periods lasting two months or more where your mood returned to normal?

No, I haven't had any breaks where my mood returned to normal. It has been a constant, steady background feeling for the entire two years and four months since it started. I haven't had even a couple of months where I felt like my old self.
Do you find that you worry excessively about these and other daily matters throughout the day, and is it hard to control or stop these worries once they start?

I don't really experience uncontrollable or excessive worry throughout the day. It is mostly just at night when I am trying to fall asleep that my mind starts racing with thoughts about my responsibilities.
During this period of low mood, have you noticed any significant changes in your appetite or weight, or have you been struggling with feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt?

Yes, my appetite has definitely decreased. I'm rarely hungry anymore, so I often skip meals during my shifts or just pick at whatever food is around. However, I wouldn't say I've been struggling with feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt.
During this long period of feeling low and exhausted, have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself, or felt that life is no longer worth living?
No, I haven't had any thoughts of hurting myself, and I've never felt like life isn't worth living. I am just feeling incredibly exhausted and weighed down by everything right now.

latest_inference.note: The patient has experienced a constant low mood ('gray heaviness'), decreased appetite, insomnia, low energy, and loss of interest in activities for over two years (two years and four months) without any symptom-free periods lasting two months or more. This clinical picture of chronic, low-grade depressive symptoms lasting more than two years fits the criteria for Dysthymia (F34.1). An acute depressive episode (F32) is ruled out due to the persistent and continuous nature of the symptoms over this long duration, and Generalized Anxiety Disorder is ruled out as the anxiety is confined to bedtime and specific responsibilities.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets the criteria for Dysthymia (F34.1) as they describe a continuous low mood ('low, gray heaviness') lasting for over two years (2 years and 4 months) without any remission period longer than two months. This chronic depressed mood is accompanied by decreased appetite, persistent insomnia, fatigue/low energy, poor concentration, and marked anhedonia, leading to significant functional impairment in academic and occupational domains. A primary sleep disorder (F51.0) is ruled out as the sleep issues are secondary to the mood disorder and racing thoughts about daily stressors, and a standard major depressive episode (F32.1) is less appropriate given the highly chronic, persistent nature of the presentation.
